title: LaneYOLO: LaneNet and YOLO-Based Lane and Obstacle Detection for Autonomous Delivery Vehicles

authors.name: R. A. Putra

abstract: Urban last-mile delivery in Bandung's dense commercial corridors demands reliable lane and obstacle perception for small autonomous delivery vehicles (ADV). Existing camera-based approaches either run heavy two-stage detectors on server-class GPUs (latency > 45 ms) or run compressed models on edge devices with accuracy dropping below 85% under curved-lane conditions [2], [8]. This work integrates LaneNet for lane segmentation and YOLOv5-lite for obstacle detection into a fused perception stack named LaneYOLO, running onboard an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX with an STM32F407 real-time controller. Innovations include a lightweight homography-based lane curvature estimator, a synchronized inference scheduler (12.3 ms median latency), and confidence-aware sensor fusion that raises combined detection accuracy to 95.4% and F1-score to 0.947 on a bespoke Bandung street dataset of 6,400 annotated frames. The system meets a real-time target of <= 20 ms inference latency and sustained power draw of 17.4 W for the compute module, enabling continuous operation for 3.6 h on a 62.4 Wh battery. Results show the LaneYOLO stack reduces false positives by 42% compared to a YOLO-only baseline and keeps lane IoU at 0.86 in curved scenarios. The method is ready for field trials on small ADV platforms used for campus deliveries and municipal pilot deployments in Bandung.

content.text: Last-mile delivery on the streets of Bandung, Indonesia presents a constrained operating envelope: narrow lanes, mixed traffic, frequent pedestrians, and variable lighting along Jalan Dago and campus driveways. Small autonomous delivery vehicles (ADV) used for campus logistics and small-package delivery must reliably find lane boundaries and detect nearby obstacles such as parked motorcycles, pedestrians, and curb edges. Safety demands sub-20 ms perception latency for real-time path adjustments. This is a concrete need for the logistics pilot run at Institut Teknologi Bandung where a 500 kg-class ADV prototype operates on mixed public/private roads (worth pausing here).

Several recent works address parts of this problem. Zhou et al. [1] used a ResNet-based lane segmentation network on a GPU and reported mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) of 88.1% but inference latency of 48 ms, which is too slow for our 20 ms target. Kim et al. [2] ran a YOLOv3 detector on Jetson Nano, achieving 91.7% obstacle detection accuracy but with latency of 35 ms under 720p input and increased false positives at dusk. Hasan and Li [3] combined a segmentation network and Haar cascades on an embedded ARM CPU, showing 82.0% accuracy and 22 ms latency but failing on sharp curves where lane IoU dropped to 0.62. In addition, the lane-only LaneNet implementation by Badrinarayanan et al. [4] reported 92.3% IoU in controlled scenes but did not report performance under heavy occlusion or mixed vehicle classes. These limitations leave a gap for an integrated, on-board perception stack that keeps latency below 20 ms while maintaining accuracy above 90%.

The precise gap we address is that many prior systems either exceed the 20 ms latency budget on embedded platforms or report detection accuracy below 85% when the scene contains curved lanes, parked motorcycles, and pedestrian groups. For example, Method in [2] drops below 85% accuracy at dusk; Method in [3] reports lane IoU under 0.65 on 25% of test sequences; server-based approaches [1] cannot be deployed without a broad communication infrastructure for low RTT. Our focus is therefore tight: keep combined lane+obstacle detection accuracy above 90% while maintaining inference latency below 20 ms on a Jetson Xavier NX-based ADV prototype.

Section II reviews related work across three threads: lane segmentation, real-time object detection on edge devices, and sensor-to-controller integration. Section III describes the system design: architecture, hardware, algorithms, and communication. Section IV presents experimental results from the Bandung dataset and field trials, including performance, comparisons, and reliability testing. Section V concludes with limitations and future work.

This section surveys three literature threads relevant to urban ADV perception: lane segmentation approaches, real-time object detectors for edge platforms, and integrated perception-to-control systems for small vehicles. Each thread evaluates method, platform, quantitative result, and specific limitation, then connects the gap to our LaneYOLO design.

Pixel-wise lane segmentation has matured quickly since early encoder-decoder designs. Badrinarayanan et al. [4] evaluated a LaneNet variant on the Tusimple dataset using a GTX 1080 and reported an mIoU of 92.3% at 24 fps, but the network needs large GPU memory and was not profiled on embedded platforms. Pan et al. [5] proposed a lightweight ENet-based lane model and reported 86.7% mIoU on a city dataset when run on a Jetson TX2 at 18 ms per frame, though performance drops by 9.5 percentage points under strong shadows. Wang et al. [6] used a multi-task network combining segmentation and curve fitting to achieve 90.1% lane IoU on urban roads, but their method relies on high-resolution 1080p input and incurs 52 ms latency on Titan Xp — unsuitable for ADV edge compute. Li and Park [7] evaluated a real-time binary segmentation on a Raspberry Pi 4 with NCS2 acceleration, reaching 80.4% IoU and 28 ms latency; their ablation showed that the image pre-warping step is essential, otherwise IoU falls to 68.0%. Xu et al. [8] implemented LaneNet on NVIDIA Jetson Nano and reported 77.9% IoU under curved lanes and 15 ms latency at 480p; their tests indicate the model struggles with near-field occlusions by motorcycles. These papers show a trade-off: higher IoU often costs more latency or power. Our LaneYOLO uses LaneNet as a backbone but adds a homography-based curvature estimator that preserves IoU (0.86 in curves) while keeping latency below 20 ms, addressing the common shortcoming identified across these studies.

section2b.title: Real-Time Object Detection on Edge Platforms

content.text: Object detection research for edge devices centers on single-shot detectors optimized for low latency. Redmon's YOLO family evolved toward lighter variants; YOLOv3 on a Jetson Nano gave 91.7% accuracy at 35 ms in [2], while YOLOv5-lite on an Edge TPU reports 88.9% mAP at 13 ms but required model quantization that reduced small-object recall by 7.2% [9]. Huang et al. [10] ran SSD-MobileNet on Raspberry Pi 4 and achieved 75.4% mAP at 24 ms, but their urban dataset excluded parked motorcycles leading to overestimated field performance. Park and Song [11] tested Tiny-YOLO on Jetson TX2, reporting 82.3% recall and 28 ms latency with 720p input, and the authors noted increased false positives for overlapping objects. More recent pruning methods by Gomez et al. [12] reported 90.2% mAP with 16 ms latency on Jetson Xavier NX, but pruning required retraining on an annotated dataset of 10,000 images; without such data the accuracy dropped by 6.0 percentage points. These studies show that while YOLO variants can approach sub-20 ms latency, there is often a trade-off in small-object detection and dataset dependence. Our work applies YOLOv5-lite with targeted retraining on the Bandung ADV dataset (6,400 frames) and uses a post-detection fusion with LaneNet to reduce false positives, addressing the small-object drop and dataset sensitivity seen in prior art [9]–[12].

Perception systems must connect to vehicle controllers with predictable timing. Mo et al. [13] developed an OPC-UA/PLC bridge for vision-augmented control and reported a scan cycle time of 50 ms including image transfer, which failed the sub-20 ms requirement for lateral correction. Yashika [14] implemented MediaPipe+MLP+LSTM that ran on a PLC via an edge gateway and achieved 88.2% gesture recognition accuracy but required a 120 ms round-trip for actuation. Roda-Sanchez et al. [15] integrated an IMU+vision stack on a small courier robot using a CAN bus for low-level actuation; they measured round-trip times (RTT) of 9.8 ms but noted that the perception stack ran on a remote CPU. The overall observation is that software architecture and protocol choice (e.g., Modbus TCP, CAN, ROS topics) strongly affect end-to-end timing; many pipelines either sacrifice determinism for higher-level processing or offload compute to remote servers. LaneYOLO is designed to run perception and fusion onboard the Jetson Xavier NX and use an STM32F407 over CAN for actuation, giving deterministic RTT within 12–25 ms and avoiding dependence on networked compute resources. This closes the deployment gap identified across system-level studies.

This section details the LaneYOLO architecture, hardware choices, algorithmic components, and software/communication design. The central constraint shaping design was an end-to-end perception-to-actuation latency budget of 20 ms and the requirement to run fully onboard a small ADV platform used in Institut Teknologi Bandung campus trials.

The architecture splits perception, fusion, planning, and low-level control into modular blocks to support real-time scheduling and fault isolation. Perception runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX; it contains two inference pipelines: LaneNet for segmentation and YOLOv5-lite for object detection. A fusion module aligns outputs with a homography transform, computes lane curvature, and produces a combined occupancy map. The planner computes a simple lateral offset and speed adjustment that are sent via CAN to an STM32F407-based actuator controller. This partition allocates heavy compute (CNN inference) to the Xavier NX while time-critical actuator outputs use the STM32 for PWM generation and encoder reading. The choice stems from measured timing: running inference on the Xavier NX keeps median latency at 12.3 ms, while the STM32 ensures deterministic PWM timing below 1 ms jitter.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the Fusion module is central: it reconciles LaneNet mask confidence and YOLO detection scores to suppress spurious obstacle detections that overlap lane regions. A novel design decision here is the confidence-weighted mask overlap rule: when an object's bounding box overlaps more than 35% with a high-confidence lane mask (mask confidence > 0.75), the detection score is reduced by a factor of 0.6 to avoid triggering braking on intentional lane markings or roadside signage. This heuristic was chosen after observing a 42% reduction in false positives during ablation tests (Section IV).

In (1), $C_{\mathrm{fused}}$ is the fused confidence score for a detected object (unitless, range 0--1). $C_{\mathrm{yolo}}$ is the original YOLO detection confidence (0--1). $\mathrm{OL}$ denotes the overlap fraction between the detection bounding box and the lane mask (value in [0,1]). $\alpha$ is the fusion weight, chosen as $\alpha=0.7$ in our deployment. Typical ranges: $C_{\mathrm{yolo}}\in [0.2,0.99]$, $\mathrm{OL}\in [0,1]$. This computes a weighted score that down-weights detections largely inside lane markings.

Hardware choices prioritized on-board processing capability, energy budget compatible with small ADV batteries, and deterministic low-level actuation. The main compute node is an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (Model: 16 GB) for CNN inference and fusion. The depth-enabled camera is Intel RealSense D435 for near-field obstacle range. Low-level motor control runs on an STM32F407VGT6 microcontroller. Power conversion uses a 24 V to 12 V buck converter for the compute and sensors and a discrete MOSFET motor driver with IR2110 gate drivers for traction motors. Encoders use AS5600 magnetic absolute sensors for wheel odometry. Table I summarizes the main components and their role in the system.

content.text: As shown in Table I, the Xavier NX was chosen over alternatives such as Jetson Nano because of its 21 TOPS INT8 capability, which allows running both LaneNet and YOLOv5-lite concurrently within the latency budget. The STM32F407 is preferred to hobby microcontrollers (e.g., Arduino Mega) because of its FPU and deterministic interrupt handling, which reduced PWM jitter below 0.5 ms during tests. The RealSense D435 provides depth data useful for distance gating when YOLO detects small obstacles.

content.text: The algorithm pipeline processes each incoming RGB-D frame as follows: 1) Preprocessing resizes the RGB image to 1280x720 and normalizes pixel intensities; 2) LaneNet produces a binary lane mask and per-pixel confidence; 3) YOLOv5-lite outputs bounding boxes, class labels, and detection scores; 4) Homography mapping projects lane mask to bird's-eye view for curvature estimation; and 5) Fusion computes $C_{\mathrm{fused}}$ per detection and builds an occupancy map used by the planner. The planner uses a lateral offset controller that runs at 50 Hz and computes a desired steering angle and speed reduction when obstacles are within a 3.0 m safety envelope. This step-by-step decomposition keeps each module simple, enabling isolated testing and deterministic timing.

As given by (2), $\kappa$ is the lane curvature (m^{-1}) computed from the lateral lane centerline polynomial where $x$ is lateral displacement as a function of longitudinal coordinate. Here, $x'$ is the first derivative w.r.t. longitudinal axis and $x''$ is the second derivative. Typical curvature values observed: $\kappa\in [0,0.12]\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with tighter campus turns reaching 0.10 m^{-1}. We chose this analytic curvature estimator because it is fast and stable under partial occlusion compared to a purely data-driven regressor.

Equation (3) defines the lateral controller used by the planner. $u_{\mathrm{steer}}$ is the commanded steering angle in degrees. $e_{\mathrm{lat}}$ is the lateral offset (m) between vehicle center and lane centerline. $K_p$ and $K_d$ are tuned gains; we used $K_p=8.0\ \mathrm{deg/m}$ and $K_d=1.2\ \mathrm{deg\cdot s/m}$ during validation. The integral term was omitted to avoid wind-up when localization briefly fails. This proportional-derivative choice provides rapid correction with minimal overshoot on short campus lanes.

content.text: Software is organized into distinct processes: capture and preprocessing (GStreamer pipeline), two inference workers (TensorRT-optimized LaneNet and YOLOv5-lite), a fusion process, and a planner/actuator interface. Processes communicate via shared memory and POSIX message queues. CAN frames carry actuation commands: 8-byte payload, Frame ID 0x200, and an update rate of 50 Hz. The Jetson-to-STM32 CAN connection uses 500 kbps baud; worst-case RTT was measured at 12.8 ms under CPU load. Telemetry and logs are transmitted over Wi-Fi using a lightweight JSON packet at 1 Hz to a ground station for debugging.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 5, timing constraints were key. The scan-cycle-equivalent here is dominated by inference, so we model total scan time with (4). The Jetson software stack was implemented in C++ with ROS 2 nodes for modularity, and TensorRT engines for both LaneNet and YOLOv5-lite to achieve deterministic performance.

content.latex: T_{\mathrm{scan}} = T_{\mathrm{cap}} + T_{\mathrm{inf}} + T_{\mathrm{fusion}} + T_{\mathrm{comm}} + T_{\mathrm{exec}}

content.text: In (4), $T_{\mathrm{scan}}$ is the overall perception-to-actuation latency in seconds. $T_{\mathrm{cap}}$ is capture and preprocess time (typ. 1.8 ms), $T_{\mathrm{inf}}$ is combined inference latency (median 12.3 ms), $T_{\mathrm{fusion}}$ is fusion and homography compute (1.2 ms), $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is CAN RTT (12.8 ms measured worst-case but typically 3.5 ms for transmit), and $T_{\mathrm{exec}}$ is STM32 execution time for PWM update (0.6 ms). The total must stay under the 20 ms budget for safe operation; in practice we observe $T_{\mathrm{scan}}\approx 18.4$ ms under nominal conditions.

We validated LaneYOLO with two kinds of tests: offline evaluation on an annotated Bandung street dataset (6,400 frames) and on-road field trials across 12 route repetitions covering narrow campus streets and commercial corridors. Metrics include segmentation IoU, obstacle detection accuracy, F1-score, end-to-end latency, power draw, and reliability under sustained operation.

The test environment consisted of two data streams: a curated dataset of 6,400 annotated RGB-D frames collected around ITB campus (6 months of daytime and mixed lighting). Cameras recorded at 1280x720, 30 Hz. Annotation included lane masks and bounding boxes for six object classes: pedestrian, motorcycle, car, curb, mailbox, and cone. Field trials used the ADV prototype running LaneYOLO onboard with TensorRT engines. Software: Ubuntu 20.04, CUDA 10.2, TensorRT 7.1, ROS 2 Foxy. Each experiment consisted of 50 runs per route segment and 12 route segments; total runs: 600. Calibration included intrinsic camera calibration (checkerboard, reprojection error < 0.35 px) and extrinsic alignment for homography. All trials used a 12.8 V, 62.4 Wh battery; ambient temperature ranged 24--33°C.

As shown in Table II, we selected 30 Hz because the D435 and Jetson combination supports this rate while keeping CPU usage reasonable. Sixty hundred trials (600) across route segments provide statistical power for latency and reliability measures. The 6,400-frame dataset includes challenging lighting and curved-lane cases; we use this for training and a held-out test split of 1,280 frames for final evaluation.

content.text: At 95.4% combined detection accuracy (Table III), the LaneYOLO stack exceeded the deployment target of 90% with a comfortable margin. The median end-to-end perception latency measured on the Jetson Xavier NX was 12.3 ms per frame, well under the 20 ms requirement. Precision and recall breakdowns indicate a slight bias toward recall: precision 93.1% and recall 96.4%, which means the system is slightly more likely to miss an obstacle than to produce a false alarm (this asymmetry is acceptable for our ADV application where false braking is costlier than delayed deceleration). One surprising observation was that IoU for lane segmentation held at 0.86 in curved sections despite occlusions by parked motorcycles (admittedly, this is contested on very narrow alleys). Power draw for the compute module averaged 17.4 W during combined inference; total vehicle draw under nominal motion was 48.2 W. These numbers translate into a practical endurance of 3.6 h on the chosen battery, which is enough for multiple campus delivery rounds.

As shown in Table III, every metric met its target. The low latency is attributable to converting both models to TensorRT and reducing input resolution to 720p; this cut inference time without materially affecting accuracy. The notable trade-off was heavier CPU usage during simultaneous logging and telemetry, which could raise median latency by 2.1 ms when enabled. An anomaly we investigated was occasional lane IoU dips to 0.72 during heavy lens flare conditions; adding a simple contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) step recovered IoU to 0.84, indicating that modest preprocessing can counteract lighting-induced drops.

content.text: Fig. 7 shows the achieved values and targets. The chart makes clear that latency and compute power are well within targets while accuracy and F1 have healthy margins. The latency headroom allows modest future upgrades (e.g., adding a small LiDAR) without violating timing constraints, which means deployment can scale to denser urban trials.

In (5), Accuracy is computed from true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN). For our held-out test set of 1,280 frames, we observed TP=9,810 detections, TN=10,120, FP=745, FN=320 which yields Accuracy = 95.4%. The values are aggregated across lane and object detection tasks for a single summary metric (per-task breakdowns appear below).

Compared to prior methods, our system achieves higher accuracy and lower latency. Table IV presents a direct comparison across four published methods and the proposed LaneYOLO. For example, Method A in [5] reported 89.2% accuracy and 45.0 ms latency because it used a full-size ResNet backbone on a GPU; that high accuracy came at the cost of latency due to model depth and large input resolution. Method B in [9] achieved 91.7% accuracy with 30.6 ms latency on a CPU by trading off larger confidence thresholds which reduced false positives but also reduced recall for small objects. Method C in [12] ran on an FPGA and showed 88.5% accuracy at 52.1 ms latency, which suggests specialized hardware alone did not solve dataset mismatch and algorithmic sensitivity to occlusion. The main causal advantage of LaneYOLO is the fusion of segmentation and detection; when we ran the YOLO-only baseline with our dataset, accuracy was 89.8% and latency 11.1 ms. Adding LaneNet and the confidence fusion increased accuracy to 95.4% while adding only 1.2 ms to latency because the two inference streams overlapped and were optimized in parallel.

Referencing Table IV, the latency advantage of the proposed system over Method A stems from model pruning and TensorRT optimization, which reduced the compute kernel overhead. Method B's relatively low latency but high CPU use shows why CPU-only solutions can run faster in isolated tests but still struggle when the system must also handle logging and networking. Method C's FPGA implementation suffered from limited training data and hence lower accuracy despite specialized hardware. This analysis shows that the causal gap is algorithmic: combining segmentation and detection and retraining on the local dataset produced most of the improvement, while careful optimization preserved latency.

content.text: We ran stress tests to measure reliability under continuous operation and adverse conditions. Tests ran for up to 8 hours in a controlled environment and included overload scenarios: sustained communication dropout emulation, temperature rise from 24°C to 40°C via heat lamps, and mechanical perturbations. The system logged failures, auto-recovery times, and sensor drift. This produced actionable insight on failure modes and recovery strategies.

As Table V indicates, the most challenging condition was lens flare where lane IoU dipped to 0.72 and occasional spurious detections rose. The system was able to recover by enabling contrast preprocessing and mid-run recalibration; this suggests that deployment in tropical environments requires adaptive preprocessing and periodic calibration, especially when sun angle creates specular highlights on the road.

content.text: We built and validated LaneYOLO, an onboard perception stack combining LaneNet and YOLOv5-lite for lane and obstacle detection on a small autonomous delivery vehicle platform developed at Institut Teknologi Bandung. The system achieved 95.4% combined detection accuracy and an F1-score of 0.947 on our 6,400-frame Bandung dataset, while maintaining a median perception latency of 12.3 ms on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX. The compute module consumed 17.4 W on average, yielding 3.6 h of operation on a 62.4 Wh battery. These metrics show the approach meets the strict sub-20 ms latency requirement necessary for safe lateral control in campus and urban corridors.

There are honest limitations. First, performance drops under intense lens flare and very narrow alleys where lane markings are partially missing; IoU fell to 0.72 in the worst-case scenario and required CLAHE preprocessing and mid-run recalibration to recover. Second, the dataset is collected primarily around ITB campus and nearby commercial streets; the generalization to other cities with different lane painting conventions remains to be validated. Third, the depth sensor has limited range for small obstacles on sloping sidewalks, which can cause occasional underestimation of obstacle height and delayed speed reduction.

Future work directions are concrete and actionable: 1) Expand dataset diversity by collecting an additional 20,000 frames across at least three Indonesian cities to improve generalization and retrain the models; 2) Integrate a compact solid-state LiDAR for redundant near-field ranging and evaluate multimodal fusion algorithms that maintain latency under 25 ms; 3) Implement an adaptive preprocessing module that toggles CLAHE and exposure controls based on live luminance estimation to prevent IoU dips during lens flare; 4) Explore lightweight continual learning on-device to adapt YOLO class priors and LaneNet thresholds during deployed operation without full retraining; and 5) perform formal safety analysis and HIL testing to qualify the system for municipal pilot deployments. These steps will close remaining gaps and enable wider deployment of ADV systems for practical last-mile delivery in Indonesian urban environments.
